summary: Provides guidelines for authors and reviewers of standards-track specifications containing MIB modules. Parts may also be useful for reviewing other MIB documents. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a checklist for people writing and checking network-management dictionaries, so they all come out clear and correct.

questions: how to review a mib module
when to use counter64 in a mib
subtitle: The rulebook IETF reviewers use to check that a MIB module is correct, clear and safe to revise.

tldr.problem: The IESG requires expert review of standards-track documents that contain MIB modules, but the SMIv2 rules were ambiguous in places and out of date in others, so reviews needed a written yardstick.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists what a MIB document must contain (boilerplate, overview, definitions, security, IANA and reference sections) and adds SMIv2 usage rules for names, data types, tables, notifications, compliance statements and revisions.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 111) and has since been updated by RFC 4841.

facts.value: 32-character recommendation set aside; 64 is a hard limit

today: RFC 4181 is a Best Current Practice and has been updated by RFC 4841. It has not been obsoleted, according to the metadata for this RFC.

sections.title: Why Reviewers Need Guidelines
sections.content:
The IESG instituted a policy of requiring expert review of IETF standards-track specifications that contain MIB modules. The reviews check that such documents follow IETF documentation practice and that the modules meet accepted quality standards, including all the syntactic and semantic requirements of SMIv2 (STD 58) in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

This memo writes down the guidelines used in those reviews. It does not intend to change MUST-level rules of existing BCPs or Internet Standards, except where they are ambiguous or contradictory. In those cases it records the generally accepted reading. In some cases it does alter SHOULD-level recommendations, where experience showed them to be suboptimal. It also picks preferred SMIv2 options where there is consensus.

Some guidelines do not apply to modules translated from SMIv1, and authors of non-standards-track or non-IETF MIB documents are encouraged to use the parts that do apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a rulebook for network dictionaries gets published, a few experts read it. This memo writes down what those experts look for, so authors can check their own work first.

sections.title: What a MIB Document Must Contain
sections.content:
The body of a MIB document MUST contain six parts: a MIB boilerplate section (a verbatim copy of the latest approved Internet-Standard Management Framework boilerplate), narrative sections, a definitions section, a Security Considerations section, an IANA Considerations section and a References section.

The narrative part MUST include an overview that describes the scope of the modules and their relationship to other standards. If the modules import definitions from other modules, or are always implemented together with others, the overview MUST say so. The definitions MUST be written in SMIv2, because SMIv1 has "Not Recommended" status and is no longer acceptable in IETF MIB modules.

The Security Considerations section MUST follow the latest approved template. Writable objects that could be disruptive if abused, and readable objects that are sensitive, MUST be listed by name with the risks explained. If a category has no risks, that MUST be stated, because silence is treated as an omission and the document goes back to the author.

The IANA section is always required. A document that creates a new name space must follow RFC 2434. A document that needs OBJECT IDENTIFIER assignments must name the registries and descriptors, using a placeholder such as XXX instead of a real number until IANA assigns it. A document with no IANA requests must say so. The memo also covers separate normative and informative reference lists, copyright notices (per RFC 3978) and the intellectual property notice (per RFC 3979).
sections.plainLanguage: Every dictionary needs the same parts, like a school report needs a title, a body and a list of sources. It also has to say what could go wrong if someone misuses it.

sections.title: Names and Where Objects Live
sections.content:
Names of standard modules MUST be unique, MUST follow the RFC 2578 syntax and MUST NOT change when a module is revised. Module names should be mnemonic.

RFC 2578 recommends that descriptors, textual convention names and labels be at most 32 characters but requires at most 64. The reviewers' consensus is that the 32-character recommendation SHOULD be set aside in favor of clarity and uniqueness, and tools SHOULD NOT warn about it by default. Going past 64 characters MUST be treated as an error.

Objects intended for operational deployment MUST NOT be registered under the experimental subtree, because it is impractical to move objects once they have seen large-scale use. The mgmt subtree is for standard objects. The MODULE-IDENTITY invocation MUST come right after IMPORTS, its value MUST be unique and, for standards-track modules, SHOULD sit under mgmt. Working-group modules MUST name the group in the ORGANIZATION clause and give its mailing list in CONTACT-INFO. Appendix C suggests a prefix-based naming scheme, such as OPT-IF-MIB with descriptors starting optIf.
sections.plainLanguage: Every word in the dictionary needs a unique, clear name, and the words must go on the right shelf. Shelves marked experimental are only for things you are just trying out.

sections.title: Choosing Data Types and Tables
sections.content:
Section 4.6.1 gives rules for picking a data type. Integer-valued enumerations REQUIRE INTEGER. For values that can go negative, Integer32 is RECOMMENDED. For non-negative values that can rise and fall, Gauge32 is RECOMMENDED, and for ones that never decrease, Unsigned32 is. Most index objects should use Unsigned32 with a range that excludes zero.

Counter32 and Counter64 must respect counter semantics. A DESCRIPTION MUST NOT require a counter to reset to zero or to reset at a given time, and a manager must not be able to ask an agent to reset one. Counters that can be disturbed should have a discontinuity indicator. The old rule limiting Counter64 to cases where a Counter32 would wrap within an hour is dropped, but Counter64 MUST still be used when such a wrap would happen. IpAddress SHOULD NOT be used in new modules in favor of InetAddress and InetAddressType from RFC 4001, and TruthValue SHOULD be used for booleans. Where a standard textual convention already has the semantics you want, you SHOULD use it.

A DESCRIPTION clause is what implementors follow, so making it clear and unambiguous is described as probably the most important job of a reviewer. For conceptual tables, an AUGMENTS clause is used for a one-to-one extension of another table's row and an INDEX clause for sparse ones. Tables with dynamic rows SHOULD have a RowStatus column, and their DESCRIPTION must say which columns are needed to activate a row. OIDs are limited to 128 sub-identifiers, so table indexing must stay within that limit.
sections.plainLanguage: Each fact in the dictionary needs the right kind of box: a counter that only goes up, a gauge that goes up and down, a yes-or-no. The rules say which box to pick, and that every entry must explain itself clearly.

sections.title: Notifications and Compliance Statements
sections.content:
For notifications, inaccessible objects MUST NOT appear in the OBJECTS clause, and the DESCRIPTION must say which instance is sent and what it means. A notification's OID MUST have a next-to-last sub-identifier of zero, so that it can be converted between an SMIv2 notification and an SMIv1 trap without loss. If an event can fire fast enough to flood the network, a mechanism MUST limit the rate, for example throttling to one notification per event source in an interval of duration T.

For conformance, every object that is not not-accessible MUST be in at least one object group, every notification MUST be in a notification group, and each standard module MUST have at least one compliance statement.

The memo flags points that are easy to overlook. A group left out of a compliance statement is unconditionally optional, but it is better to list it in a GROUP clause stating that it is optional. Read-write or read-create objects without a MIN-ACCESS of read-only force implementations to support write access, which authors often do not intend. A read-only compliance statement supports monitoring but not configuration, so modules meant for both should provide a read-only and a full statement.
sections.plainLanguage: If the dictionary can shout an alarm, it must not shout so often that everyone gets drowned out. And it must say clearly which entries every device has to support and which are optional.

sections.title: Revising a MIB Module
sections.content:
When a module is revised, the MODULE-IDENTITY must be updated: LAST-UPDATED is set to the revision time, and a new REVISION clause with the same UTC time describes the changes. The module name MUST NOT change (except to fix typos), existing definitions MUST NOT be removed even if obsolete, and descriptors and OBJECT IDENTIFIER values MUST NOT be changed or reused.

The point is backward compatibility of two kinds. Unchanged OIDs keep "over the wire" compatibility between agents and managers on different revisions. Unchanged names and kept definitions keep "compilation" compatibility for modules that import from the revised one.

The memo corrects RFC 2578 and RFC 2579 on one point: labels of named numbers and named bits MUST NOT be changed in IETF modules, since DEFVAL clauses elsewhere may use them. Objects and notifications MUST NOT be added to or removed from an existing group. In exceptional cases the rules can be waived, but then the change and its justification MUST be thoroughly documented.
sections.plainLanguage: When you update the dictionary you can add new words, but you must never erase or rename old ones, because other books already point to them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is short. Deploying a MIB module can create security risks that would not otherwise exist, so authors and reviewers must make sure documents comply with the approved security guidelines so that all such risks are disclosed.

The IANA Considerations section notes that the memo only describes what a MIB document's IANA section must contain. It does not ask IANA to update any registry or create a new one.

Appendix A turns the guidelines into a ten-item review checklist, running from Internet-Draft boilerplate and abstract through the MIB boilerplate, security and IANA sections, references, copyright and IPR notices, and finally the technical content, where it stresses reading the document as an implementor would.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything that lets you read or change settings on a device can be misused, so every dictionary must say clearly where the dangers are.
